purpose: This medication is used to lower high potassium levels in your blood, a condition called hyperkalemia. High potassium can be dangerous and affect how your heart works. Your doctor may prescribe this if your kidneys are not removing enough potassium on their own.
how_it_works: Think of this medicine like a tiny sponge that travels through your digestive system. As it moves through your gut, it absorbs extra potassium and holds onto it. Then, when you have a bowel movement, the potassium is removed from your body along with the medicine.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects involve your stomach and digestion, such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, stomach cramps, or diarrhea. Some people may also notice a loss of appetite. These effects are usually mild but let your doctor know if they bother you.
warnings: This medicine can sometimes cause serious constipation or a rare but serious bowel problem called intestinal necrosis (tissue damage in the gut), especially after surgery. It can also lower other minerals in your blood like calcium and magnesium. Do not take it at the same time as other oral medications, as it can interfere with them. Tell your doctor if you have a history of bowel problems or are on a low-sodium diet, since this medicine does contain sodium.
typical_dosing: The typical adult dose is 15 grams (about one tablespoon) taken by mouth one to four times a day, usually mixed with water or a sweet liquid. It can also be given as an enema (rectally) at a dose of 30 to 50 grams. Your doctor will decide the right dose and form for you based on your potassium levels.
